prompt:
Pixel-art sprite sheet, single image, fully transparent background.

SUBJECT: the tall, heavily muscled African-American professional basketball
player in the attached reference image. Match that character exactly, his face
above all: dark brown skin, a shaved head, a broad, full, rounded face with
full cheeks, a heavy brow, a broad nose and full lips, exactly as the reference
draws them. He is easy-going and good-humoured -- a star playing on easy mode
against easy opponents, relaxed, amused and enjoying himself, with a confident
half-smile as his resting expression, never a scowl. Heavy shoulders and arms,
a blue sleeveless basketball jersey with a yellow number 34, blue shorts with
white and yellow trim, white high-top sneakers with blue and yellow flashes
over white socks. Identical colours, identical proportions, identical build and
identical height as the reference, in every frame.

LAYOUT: one horizontal row of 5 frames of equal width, evenly spaced. No
borders, no frame numbers, no labels, no background, no drop shadows.

POSE GUIDE: TWO images are attached, and they do different jobs.

The COLOUR image of the character is the only authority on WHO HE IS. His
colours, his proportions, his build, his height, his face, his kit and the
drawing style all come from that image and from the SUBJECT above, and nothing
below changes any of them. It does NOT decide which way he faces: in that
drawing he is turned toward the right edge, and in this sheet he is not.

The other image is a POSE GUIDE: a plain black stick figure on a white
background, five figures standing in a row on one ground line, in the same
left-to-right order as the FRAMES listed below. The Nth figure in the pose
guide is the pose for the Nth frame. Take the GEOMETRY from it and only the
geometry: where each foot stands on the ground line, how deeply the knees are
bent, how far the shoulder line is tilted, how high the dribbling hand is and
how far out from his centre line it reaches, and which way his face points.
Where the words below and the pose guide describe the same thing, they agree;
the pose guide is the exact version of it. The four dribbling figures are MEANT
to look almost alike: the differences between them are small, and they should
stay small.

THE HANDS ON THE POSE GUIDE are drawn too. The FLAT hand with its fingers
spread out sideways is the dribbling hand: palm to the floor, at exactly that
height. The NARROW hand with its fingers pointing down at the floor is the free
hand, palm turned in toward his leg. Each is ONE drawing, moved from frame to
frame.

THE HEAD ON THE POSE GUIDE: the small TRIANGLE in the middle of the face,
pointing straight down, is his nose, and the two small ovals on either side of
the head are BOTH of his ears. His face points STRAIGHT OUT OF THE PICTURE AT
THE VIEWER in every frame: nose in the middle of his face, both eyes seen, both
ears showing equally. The upright line down the face marks its centre and the
level line his eyes. His head is shaved smooth; the pose guide draws no hair on
it.

Draw the character from the colour reference standing in those positions. The
pose guide is an instruction, not artwork: its thin flat lines, its joint dots,
its white background, its circular head, its triangle, its ovals and its face
lines are NOT part of the drawing and must not appear anywhere in it.

CAMERA: locked off. Identical distance and eye level in every frame. The
character must be exactly the same height in every frame, and the same height
as in the reference image — do not zoom, crop, recompose or rescale between
frames. All frames share one ground line: the soles of the feet touch the same
horizontal line in every frame.

VIEW: front view, facing the viewer, squared to camera: his chest, his hips and
his face all point straight out of the picture, both shoulders the same
distance from the camera, the number on his jersey in the middle of his chest.
A relaxed, low athletic stance: knees bent, feet planted a little wider than
his shoulders, holding that crouch steadily.

CRITICAL: exactly ONE hand dribbles — the hand nearer the LEFT EDGE of the
picture, on the VIEWER'S LEFT — in all four frames. The other hand never
dribbles.

THIS IS A CALM, EASY DRIBBLE, AND HIS BODY HARDLY MOVES. He holds one steady
low crouch in all four frames: his head sits at almost the same height in every
frame, his shoulders stay almost level, his back stays almost upright. The only
thing that plainly moves is the dribbling FOREARM AND HAND, bouncing the ball
from the elbow and the wrist. Keep every other difference between the frames
SMALL — a slight dip, a slight rise — never a lunge, a heave or a deep knee
bend.

THE DRIBBLING HAND is flat and open: palm facing DOWN at the floor, fingers
spread and straight, the shape of a hand resting on the top of a ball. DRAW THE
SAME HAND FOUR TIMES — the same shape, the same spread of the fingers, the same
angle to the floor — simply moved up and down from frame to frame. It travels
in one short straight line OUTSIDE HIS HIP, beside his thigh, with clear
background between his forearm and his jersey.

THE HAND'S FOUR HEIGHTS, IN ORDER, all of them low: in the LOWEST frame it is
beside his KNEE; in the RISING frame it is a little higher, on his LOWER THIGH;
in the HIGHEST frame it is just ABOVE THE HEM of his shorts, and never higher
than that; in the DRIVING DOWN frame it is level with the HEM. Each frame has
the hand at a DIFFERENT height, but the whole travel is short: from the knee to
just above the hem, and no further.

THE FREE HAND IS NOT DRIBBLING AND DOES NOT COPY IT. That arm simply hangs:
upper arm against his ribs, elbow almost straight, and the hand hanging from
the wrist with the PALM TURNED IN toward his thigh, fingers straight, relaxed
and a little apart, pointing down at the floor. It is ONE DRAWING REPEATED IN
ALL FOUR FRAMES, held just clear of his leg so the whole hand shows against the
background.

HIS FEET ARE ONE DRAWING REPEATED IN ALL FOUR FRAMES: both shoes in the same
place on the floor, the same distance apart, at the same angle, as if traced
from one frame into the next three. The small dip and rise come from his knees,
never from moving his feet.

HE LOOKS STRAIGHT AT THE VIEWER IN ALL FOUR FRAMES: both eyes seen, his nose in
the middle of his face, both ears showing. The character reference shows him
turned toward the RIGHT edge with his head in profile; that is how he stood for
that drawing, NOT this pose, so do not copy the turn. His head never turns
toward the dribbling hand or toward either edge of the picture. At most it tips
a hair toward the dribbling side in the LOWEST frame.

FRAMES, left to right:
1. CALIBRATION POSE: standing straight upright, feet shoulder-width apart, arms
   hanging relaxed at his sides, facing the viewer, in the plain neutral
   standing pose from the reference image. This exact pose appears as the first
   frame of every sheet in this set and must be drawn identically every time.
2. LOWEST, the push landed. The dribbling hand is at its lowest, beside his
   KNEE, arm almost straight, wrist loose. He has dipped a little into his
   crouch, the shoulder on the dribbling side a touch lower than the other. The
   free hand hangs at his side.
3. RISING. The hand has come up a little, to his LOWER THIGH, the elbow
   starting to bend. His body is almost exactly as in the LOWEST frame, a touch
   less dipped. The free hand hangs at his side.
4. HIGHEST. The hand is at the top of its short travel, just ABOVE THE HEM of
   his shorts, elbow bent, ready to push down again. His shoulders are level
   and his crouch is at its shallowest, but he is still in the same low
   athletic stance. His head is level, looking straight at the viewer. The free
   hand hangs at his side.
5. DRIVING DOWN. His knees give a little and the hand pushes down, still level
   with the HEM, following the body down. Almost the same pose as the RISING
   frame, with the hand a little higher. The free hand hangs at his side.

This row is a seamless loop: frame 5 must flow back into frame 2 with no jump.

The four frames are nearly the same picture with the dribbling forearm and hand
at four different heights and his body dipping and rising only slightly.
Subtle, relaxed, steady: this is how he waits with the ball.

STYLE: VGA-era 256-colour DOS-game pixel art, drawn pixel by pixel — NOT a
modern illustration with a pixel filter over it. The limits below are the look;
keep all of them: - At most THREE tones per material: a base, one darker
shadow, one lighter highlight. Hard edges between the tones. - NO gradients, NO
soft or airbrushed shading, NO glow, NO bloom, and NO anti-aliasing anywhere —
not on the outline, not between tones, not around the silhouette. - Where a
tone change needs softening, use visible ORDERED DITHER — a checkerboard of the
two tones. Dither, never blend. - Chunky square pixels on one consistent grid,
plainly visible at full size. - A bold dark outline around the silhouette and
around the major forms inside it. The background must be fully transparent
(alpha 0) with no haze, glow or soft fringe around the silhouette. Output a
wide landscape image.

The character is NOT holding a basketball in any frame — the ball is drawn
separately by the game.
